triage.name: HPV
triage.reason: Common infection with a clear presentation (genital warts, abnormal cervical screening) reachable by history, exam and testing; counseling and cancer-prevention implications make it a strong case.

demographics: Nearly all sexually active people acquire HPV soon after becoming sexually active
Most infections are asymptomatic and clear within 1–2 years
Genital warts are most common in young adults in their late teens through twenties
HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer is more common in men and in adults in their 50s–60s
Cervical precancer and cancer are detected through screening, so presentation often follows an abnormal Pap or HPV test

risk_factors.text: Sexual activity with one or more partners
New sexual partner or multiple partners
Tobacco use (increases persistence and cancer risk)
History of another sexually transmitted infection

exposures: Unprotected vaginal, anal, or oral sex
Skin-to-skin genital contact with an infected partner

chief_complaints.text: I noticed some bumps down there
My doctor said my Pap test was abnormal
I have a lump or growth in my genital area
I have no symptoms, but my partner told me they have HPV
I have a sore or bump in my mouth or throat

hpi.onset: Gradual; warts appear weeks to months after exposure, while high-risk HPV is usually detected only on screening and may have been present for years
hpi.duration: Warts may be present for weeks to months before evaluation; high-risk HPV infection is often longstanding and asymptomatic
hpi.progression: Warts may stay the same, grow in size or number, or resolve on their own; high-risk HPV usually clears without symptoms, but persistent infection can cause precancerous cell changes over years
hpi.location: Genital area (vulva, vagina, cervix, penis, scrotum), anus or perianal skin, and sometimes the mouth or throat
hpi.quality: Small bumps or clusters that may be raised or flat, smooth or cauliflower-like; usually painless
hpi.severity: Mild; most people have no pain or systemic symptoms
hpi.timing: Warts are persistent and may slowly change over weeks to months; high-risk HPV has no symptoms
aggravating: Friction or irritation of the area

associated_symptoms.text: Visible bumps or warts in the genital or anal area
Itching or irritation around the warts
Mild bleeding or discomfort with intercourse if warts are irritated
Abnormal cervical screening result (Pap or HPV test)

pertinent_negatives: Flu-like illness with fever and swollen glands at the time of exposure
Unexplained weight loss or night sweats

positives.text: Small bumps or warts in the genital or anal area
Itching or irritation of the affected skin
Abnormal Pap or HPV test result

negatives: Vaginal bleeding between periods or after sex
argues_against: Cervical cancer with bleeding or pelvic pain

positives.text: Persistent sore throat or lump in the throat

atypical.how_it_differs: People with HIV or on immunosuppressants are more likely to have persistent HPV, larger or more numerous warts, and faster progression to precancer or cancer.
Warts may grow larger during pregnancy due to immune and hormonal changes, and can bleed or obstruct the birth canal; HPV can rarely be transmitted to the newborn.
New HPV detection may reflect reactivation of a remote infection rather than a new exposure; HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer is more common in this group.

Genital warts in children raise concern for sexual abuse, though non-sexual transmission (e.g., perinatal, autoinoculation, fomites) can occur; respiratory papillomatosis can present with hoarseness or stridor.

general.moderate: Well-appearing, comfortable; may be anxious about the diagnosis
general.severe: Ill-appearing only if there is a large or secondarily infected lesion or an HPV-associated tumor
general.critical: Toxic-appearing only with a secondary complication such as a large obstructing or infected lesion

findings.maneuver: Inspect the vulva, vagina, penis, scrotum, perineum and perianal skin in good light
findings.finding: Single or clustered soft, fleshy, raised or flat papules, sometimes cauliflower-like

findings.maneuver: Palpate the lesions and ask about pain
Inspect the genital mucosa for breaks in the skin
findings.finding: No ulcers, vesicles or crusted erosions

findings.maneuver: Perform a speculum exam of the vagina and cervix
findings.finding: Normal-appearing vaginal and cervical mucosa without visible lesions

findings.maneuver: Inspect the cervix and perform a bimanual exam
findings.finding: No visible cervical lesion, no cervical motion tenderness, no adnexal mass

findings.maneuver: Inspect the perianal skin and perform a digital rectal exam when anal involvement is suspected
findings.finding: No perianal warts, mass or tenderness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral cavity, oropharynx and palpate the neck
findings.finding: Wart-like lesion, mucosal irregularity or neck mass

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin beyond the anogenital area
findings.finding: No rash, vesicles or other lesions

labs.caveat: Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before colposcopy, biopsy or treatment of cervical precancer.
Usually normal. Mild leukocytosis only if a large wart is secondarily infected.

imaging.preferred_when: Abnormal cervical screening (HPV-positive or abnormal cytology)

findings.text: Acetowhite epithelium at the transformation zone
Abnormal vessels or atypical transformation zone suggesting high-grade lesion
Normal-appearing cervix with no acetowhite lesion (no visible abnormality)

imaging.preferred_when: Anal HPV or abnormal anal cytology, especially in immunocompromised patients

findings.text: Acetowhite lesions in the anal canal or perianal skin

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer (persistent neck mass or throat lesion)

findings.text: Enlarged cystic or solid cervical lymph node
Primary mucosal lesion in the oropharynx (tonsil or base of tongue)

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected invasive cervical or anal cancer, or staging

findings.text: Cervical mass with parametrial or vaginal extension
Anal or perianal mass with sphincter involvement
Pulmonary nodules suggesting metastasis (in advanced HPV-associated cancer)

initial.why: Detects high-risk HPV types and guides screening and follow-up
initial.only_if: cervical cancer screening is due or cytology is abnormal

initial.why: Detects precancerous or cancerous cervical cell changes
initial.only_if: cervical cancer screening is due or HPV test is positive

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy before colposcopy, biopsy or treatment
Immunosuppression increases HPV persistence and cancer risk and changes screening intervals
initial.only_if: risk factors for HIV or newly diagnosed HPV-related disease

confirmatory.why: Confirms and grades cervical precancer (CIN) when screening is abnormal
Confirms the diagnosis when lesions are atypical, pigmented, ulcerated or fail treatment

confirmatory.test: Anal cytology and high-resolution anoscopy with biopsy
confirmatory.why: Confirms anal precancer in high-risk or immunocompromised patients
confirmatory.only_if: anal HPV, abnormal anal cytology or symptoms

supporting.test: Other STI testing (chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, trichomonas)
supporting.why: Co-infections are common and require treatment

supporting.test: Biopsy of oral or neck lesion
supporting.why: Confirms HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer when a persistent mass or mucosal lesion is present
supporting.only_if: persistent neck mass, sore throat or oral lesion

not_indicated.why: Not used clinically; cannot distinguish current from past infection
Routine blood counts are not needed for uncomplicated HPV or genital warts
Liver and metabolic tests are not part of HPV workup
Inflammatory markers are not useful for HPV or warts
Not indicated unless invasive HPV-associated cancer is suspected

decision_points: Pregnancy test before colposcopy, biopsy or treatment of cervical precancer in anyone who could be pregnant
Visible genital warts are diagnosed clinically; biopsy only if atypical, pigmented, ulcerated or refractory
Abnormal cervical screening requires colposcopy with biopsy to grade the lesion before treatment
Immunocompromised patients need more frequent screening and lower thresholds for anoscopy or colposcopy

differential.name: Genital herpes
differential.why_considered: Genital lesions in a sexually active patient; HSV is the most common cause of painful genital ulcers and can be mistaken for warts when atypical.
differential.trigger: Painful grouped vesicles or ulcers with a prodrome of tingling or burning

history: Prodrome of tingling, burning or itching before lesions appear
Painful lesions, often with dysuria
Flu-like illness with fever and tender groin nodes at first episode
Recurrent episodes in the same location
exam: Grouped vesicles or shallow, punched-out ulcers with an erythematous base
Lesions may be bilateral and extensive in primary infection
labs: Positive HSV-1 or HSV-2 PCR from a swab of the lesion base
Type-specific HSV serology if the lesion has healed

differential.name: Molluscum contagiosum
differential.why_considered: Small, smooth, skin-colored bumps in the genital area that can look like flat warts.

history: Lesions are usually painless and not itchy
Spread by skin-to-skin contact, including sexual contact in adults
exam: Firm, dome-shaped papules with a central dimple (umbilication)
Lesions are smooth rather than verrucous or cauliflower-like
Often found on the thighs, lower abdomen and genital skin
labs: Diagnosis is clinical; biopsy shows intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (Henderson-Paterson bodies) if needed

differential.name: Condyloma lata (secondary syphilis)
differential.why_considered: Raised, moist anogenital lesions that can be mistaken for genital warts; syphilis is a must-not-miss STI.
differential.trigger: Moist, flat, broad-based anogenital papules with a rash on the palms and soles

history: Recent painless genital ulcer (chancre) that resolved
Diffuse rash involving palms and soles
Fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy
exam: Broad, flat, moist, gray-white papules (condyloma lata) in the anogenital area
Copper-colored maculopapular rash on trunk, palms and soles
labs: Positive nontreponemal test (RPR or VDRL) with confirmatory treponemal test
Dark-field microscopy or PCR of lesion exudate

differential.name: Pearly penile papules
differential.why_considered: Small, regular bumps on the coronal sulcus of the penis that patients may mistake for warts.

history: Present for years, unchanged
Not sexually transmitted; no partner history
exam: 1–2 mm smooth, dome-shaped papules in one or two rows along the coronal sulcus
Uniform in size and color, no cauliflower appearance

differential.name: Seborrheic keratosis
differential.why_considered: Pigmented or raised skin lesions that can resemble warts, especially on the vulva or perianal skin.

history: Slowly growing, often asymptomatic
Usually in older adults
exam: Well-demarcated, 'stuck-on' plaque with a waxy or verrucous surface
May have comedo-like openings or a horn cyst
labs: Biopsy shows horn cysts and basaloid proliferation if diagnosis is uncertain

differential.name: Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia or vulvar cancer
differential.why_considered: HPV-associated precancer or cancer can present as a vulvar lesion or persistent pruritus that may be mistaken for warts.
differential.trigger: Persistent vulvar pruritus, bleeding, or an ulcerated or pigmented lesion that does not respond to wart treatment

history: Persistent vulvar itching, burning or bleeding
Lesion that enlarges or ulcerates despite treatment
History of cervical or anal HPV-related disease
exam: Raised, ulcerated, pigmented or indurated vulvar lesion
labs: Biopsy showing high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion or invasive carcinoma
p16 immunohistochemistry positive in HPV-associated tumors
imaging: MRI pelvis to assess local extent and nodal involvement if invasive

differential.name: Cervical cancer
differential.why_considered: High-risk HPV is the cause of nearly all cervical cancers; abnormal screening or symptoms may be attributed to HPV alone.
differential.trigger: Abnormal cervical screening with postcoital bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding or pelvic pain

history: Postcoital or intermenstrual vaginal bleeding
Watery or bloody vaginal discharge
Pelvic pain or pain with intercourse
exam: Visible cervical lesion, friable cervix or contact bleeding
Palpable cervical mass or parametrial thickening on bimanual exam
labs: Positive high-risk HPV test with abnormal cytology
Biopsy confirming invasive squamous cell or adenocarcinoma
imaging: MRI pelvis showing cervical mass with parametrial or vaginal extension
PET-CT for staging if locally advanced

differential.name: Oropharyngeal cancer
differential.why_considered: HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer can present with a persistent neck mass or sore throat that may be attributed to a benign process.
differential.trigger: Persistent unilateral sore throat, globus, or a painless neck mass lasting more than 2–3 weeks

history: Persistent unilateral sore throat or ear pain
Painless neck mass that does not resolve with antibiotics
Tobacco and alcohol use increase risk
exam: Enlarged, firm cervical lymph node, often level II–III
Mucosal lesion or asymmetry in the tonsil or base of tongue
labs: Biopsy of the primary or neck node showing squamous cell carcinoma, p16-positive
imaging: CT or MRI neck showing cystic or solid lymph node and primary lesion

severity.mild: Asymptomatic HPV infection detected on screening, or a few small, painless genital warts without functional impact.
severity.moderate: Multiple or larger genital warts causing itching, irritation, or psychological distress; or low-grade cervical precancer (CIN 1) on colposcopy.
severity.severe: Extensive or recurrent warts, high-grade cervical or anal precancer (CIN 2/3 or AIN 2/3), or an HPV-associated cancer that is localized and treatable.
severity.critical: Invasive HPV-associated cancer with local invasion, obstruction, or metastasis; or respiratory papillomatosis causing airway obstruction.

red_flags.finding: Persistent vulvar, vaginal, or anal bleeding or ulceration
red_flags.meaning: Possible invasive HPV-associated cancer; needs urgent biopsy and gynecologic or oncologic evaluation

red_flags.finding: Painless neck mass or persistent unilateral sore throat lasting more than 2–3 weeks
red_flags.meaning: Possible HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer; needs ENT evaluation and imaging

red_flags.finding: Large or rapidly growing warts that obstruct the birth canal or urinary stream
red_flags.meaning: May require urgent intervention, especially in pregnancy

red_flags.finding: Hoarseness or stridor in an infant or young child
red_flags.meaning: Possible recurrent respiratory papillomatosis with airway involvement; urgent airway evaluation

red_flags.finding: Immunosuppression with extensive or rapidly progressive anogenital lesions
red_flags.meaning: Higher risk of persistent HPV and progression to precancer or cancer; lower threshold for biopsy and specialist referral

complications.name: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (precancer)
clues: Abnormal Pap test or HPV test

complications.name: Anal cancer
clues: Abnormal anal cytology in an immunocompromised patient

complications.name: Oropharyngeal cancer
clues: p16-positive squamous cell carcinoma on biopsy

complications.name: Secondary bacterial infection of warts
clues: Pain, redness, purulent discharge from warts

special_populations.differences: People with HIV, transplant recipients, or those on chronic steroids are more likely to have persistent HPV, larger and more numerous warts, faster progression to precancer or cancer, and require more frequent screening and lower thresholds for biopsy.

Warts may grow larger due to immune and hormonal changes, can bleed or obstruct the birth canal, and may require treatment before delivery; HPV can rarely be transmitted to the newborn, causing respiratory papillomatosis.

Genital warts in children raise concern for sexual abuse, though non-sexual transmission (perinatal, autoinoculation, fomites) can occur; respiratory papillomatosis can present with hoarseness or stridor.
New HPV detection may reflect reactivation of a remote infection rather than a new exposure; HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer is more common in this group.

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any bumps, warts, or growths in your genital or anal area?
key_questions.looking_for: Visible warts or growths; low-risk HPV types cause genital warts

key_questions.question: When did you first notice them, and have they changed in size or number?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months; warts may stay stable, grow, or resolve

key_questions.question: Are the bumps painful, itchy, or bleeding?
key_questions.looking_for: Usually painless; itching or irritation sometimes; bleeding suggests irritation or another cause

key_questions.question: Have you had an abnormal Pap test or a positive HPV test?
key_questions.looking_for: Abnormal cervical screening is the usual way high-risk HPV is detected

key_questions.question: When was your last cervical cancer screening, and what were the results?
key_questions.looking_for: Screening history and follow-up; guides need for colposcopy

key_questions.question: Are you sexually active? Do you have vaginal, anal, or oral sex?
key_questions.looking_for: HPV spreads by skin-to-skin sexual contact, including oral and anal sex

key_questions.question: How many sexual partners have you had, and have you had a new partner recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Multiple or new partners increase exposure risk

key_questions.question: Do you use condoms? How consistently?
key_questions.looking_for: Condoms reduce but do not eliminate transmission

key_questions.question: Have you been vaccinated against HPV? How many doses?
key_questions.looking_for: Vaccination protects against the types that cause warts and most HPV cancers

key_questions.question: Have you or any partner ever had an STI, including herpes, HIV, chlamydia, gonorrhea, or syphilis?
key_questions.looking_for: Co-infections are common and change management

key_questions.question: Do you have HIV, or are you on medicines that suppress your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression increases persistence and cancer risk

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or use tobacco?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco increases HPV persistence and cancer risk

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy affects treatment choices and is required before procedures

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any sores, blisters, or ulcers in the genital area?
key_questions.looking_for: Painful ulcers suggest herpes, not HPV

key_questions.question: Any unusual vaginal or penile discharge, burning with urination, or pelvic pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Discharge or dysuria suggests another STI or UTI

key_questions.question: Have you had a persistent sore throat, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or a lump in your neck?
Any unexplained weight loss, night sweats, or fevers?
key_questions.looking_for: Constitutional symptoms suggest malignancy or systemic illness

key_questions.question: Any postcoital, intermenstrual, or postmenopausal bleeding?
key_questions.looking_for: Possible cervical or vulvar cancer; needs urgent evaluation

reasoning_points: HPV is the most common sexually transmitted infection and most infections are asymptomatic and clear within 1–2 years
Low-risk HPV types (6 and 11) cause genital warts; high-risk types (16, 18, and others) cause cervical, anal, oropharyngeal, vulvar, vaginal, and penile cancers
Genital warts are diagnosed clinically by inspection; biopsy is reserved for atypical, pigmented, ulcerated, or treatment-refractory lesions
High-risk HPV is detected by cervical HPV testing and cytology (Pap), with colposcopy and biopsy to grade precancer
Pregnancy must be excluded before colposcopy, biopsy, or treatment of cervical precancer
HIV testing is indicated because immunosuppression increases HPV persistence and cancer risk
The differential includes genital herpes (painful vesicles/ulcers), molluscum contagiosum (umbilicated papules), condyloma lata of secondary syphilis (must not miss), and HPV-associated cancers
HPV cannot be cured with antivirals; management focuses on treating warts, treating precancer, preventing cancer with screening, and vaccination

easy: Young sexually active adult with classic painless, cauliflower-like genital warts on inspection
No systemic symptoms and no genital ulcers or discharge
Abnormal cervical screening with positive high-risk HPV test in an otherwise healthy patient
medium: Asymptomatic patient with a positive high-risk HPV test and normal or mildly abnormal cytology
Flat or small warts that are hard to see without good lighting or acetic acid
Patient with coexisting STI symptoms such as discharge or dysuria
Immunocompetent patient with recurrent warts after treatment
hard: Immunocompromised patient (HIV, transplant, chronic steroids) with extensive or rapidly progressive anogenital lesions
Pregnant patient with large warts that bleed or obstruct the birth canal
Older adult with a persistent painless neck mass or unilateral sore throat suggesting HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer
Patient with postcoital bleeding and an abnormal Pap suggesting invasive cervical cancer
Child with genital warts raising concern for sexual abuse versus non-sexual transmission
Lesion that is pigmented, ulcerated, or fails treatment and requires biopsy to exclude vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia or cancer
